title: What Is Conceptual Understanding Good For?
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane, frustrated by his own vague goals when teaching "for conceptual understanding," sets out to name specific, concrete purposes the concept actually serves, since he found no single existing resource that offered clear examples rather than fuzzy statements about "making connections." He identifies five distinct functions: course correction (a conceptual grasp of integer addition or circle geometry helps students recover when a hazy procedure fails); flexibility (recognizing 103 minus 96 are 7 apart avoids a clunky standard algorithm); explaining why a procedure works (deriving the circle area formula so it isn't "made up out of nowhere"); choosing which strategy applies to an unfamiliar problem; and connecting new material to prior knowledge (percents as fractions with a denominator of 100). Kane then uses this framework to answer a separate long-standing question -- whether concepts or procedures should come first -- arguing the order depends on which function is in play: concepts-first when the goal is course correction or connecting to prior knowledge, procedures-first when the goal is explaining why or choosing a strategy, and either order when the goal is flexibility. He closes by framing the real value of the exercise as giving him concrete criteria to judge whether a conceptual-understanding activity is actually worthwhile, rather than continuing to design lessons around fuzzy, ungrounded goals.
points: Kane's five functions of conceptual understanding -- course correction, flexibility, explaining why, choosing a strategy, connecting to prior knowledge -- replace vague goals ("making connections") with concrete, checkable purposes.

He resolves the long-standing concepts-vs-procedures-first debate by function rather than by blanket rule: concepts first for course correction and prior-knowledge connections, procedures first for explaining why or choosing a strategy.

A concrete example of the \"flexibility\" function: recognizing 103 and 96 are 7 apart lets a student skip the standard subtraction algorithm entirely, illustrating conceptual understanding as an alternate, more efficient path rather than a supplement to procedure.

Kane explicitly frames the framework's value as practical: it gives him criteria to judge whether a specific conceptual-understanding activity is worth doing, rather than continuing with fuzzy, ungrounded goals.
quotes: What is the point of conceptual understanding? I often find myself teaching something in the name of conceptual understanding but without a very clear goal of what I want students to learn.
Humans forget things. If students only have a procedural understanding of something, when the procedure gets hazy they are prone to make silly mistakes.
Standard algorithms are great in lots of situations, but they are also inefficient in others. Conceptual understanding can offer students an alternate path in certain situations.
Students want to feel like math makes sense and to know why a rule works or why a procedure is what it is.
New knowledge sticks best when it's connected to prior learning. Conceptual understanding is the stuff that connects concepts and creates those links.
I want to have clear goals when I try to teach conceptual understanding to ensure students are learning something useful and not foundering with fuzzy knowledge.
